Research

My research uses regression modeling and survey methods to study suicide prevention, gastroenterology, infectious disease, and population health. Selected projects are below, grouped by theme.

Suicide & Firearms

Firearm Access and Suicide Rates: A Cross-National Analysis

Research Assistant · Columbia University Irving Medical Center · Oct 2025 – Oct 2026
With Dr. Tomer Levy and Dr. Larkin McReynolds

Question: Is civilian firearm prevalence associated with suicide rates across countries, and does the association differ by age and sex?

Data: WHO mortality and UN demographic data for 62 countries (2017–2021). This is more than 20,000 sex- and age-stratified observations, linked to national firearm ownership indicators.

Methods: Negative binomial regression with cluster-robust standard errors, plus interaction analyses by age and sex. All in R (tidyverse, ggplot2).

My role: I ran all of the statistical analyses, built a reproducible pipeline to clean, harmonize, and merge the datasets, and made the publication figures.

Output: Manuscript in preparation. First-author oral presentation at the National Research Conference for the Prevention of Firearm-Related Harms (Dec 2026).

Suicide Methods Across Decades and Countries

Research Assistant · Columbia University Irving Medical Center · Jul 2026 – Present
With Dr. Tomer Levy and Dr. Larkin McReynolds

I’m leading the statistical design of a new cross-national study comparing suicide methods across decades and countries.

Clinical Research & Real-World Data

Incontinence After BPH Surgery: An EHR Analysis

Research Intern · VA Boston Research Student Summer Institute · May – Aug 2024
In collaboration with Boston Scientific

Question: How do incontinence rates change after surgery for benign prostatic hyperplasia?

Data: U.S. electronic health record data.

My role: I managed project planning, including endpoint design, and drafted the statistical exhibits.

Findings: Post-surgical incontinence rates went down over time. The project also showed the limits of real-world data for determining whether symptoms had resolved.

Treatment Patterns in Eosinophilic Esophagitis

Research Assistant · Columbia University Irving Medical Center · Jan – Aug 2026
With Dr. Sydney Pomenti and Dr. David Katzka

Question: How do eosinophilic esophagitis experts approach patients who are referred to them for consultation?

Data: A cross-sectional survey of 52 EoE experts covering provider characteristics, referral patterns, perceived causes of treatment failure, diagnostic approaches, and prior therapies.

Methods: Statistical analysis in R (gtsummary).

My role: I finalized the manuscript’s reported statistics, tables, and figures.

Output: Co-author, Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics (2026). Read the paper

Infectious Disease & Antimicrobial Resistance

Public Perceptions of Antimicrobial Resistance (Master’s Thesis)

McGill University → Columbia Mailman · May 2023 – Present
With Dr. Lysanne Campeau (McGill) and Dr. Lori Lerner (VA Boston)

Question: How aware is the public of the antimicrobial resistance crisis, and which everyday behaviors contribute to it?

Data: A survey I designed and implemented, with 199 completed responses from the U.S. and Canada.

Methods: Linear regression.

Findings: Participants were generally unaware of the AMR crisis and took few specific actions to avoid resistance.

Output: Poster at the 2025 American Urological Association Annual Meeting. A manuscript is in preparation, and I’m now extending this dataset into my master’s thesis, where I’m leading the analysis.

Tick-Borne Disease in Rural Agricultural Counties

Research Intern · Bassett Healthcare Network (NYCAMH) · Jun – Jul 2026
With Dr. Amanda Roome and Dr. Thelma Mielenz

Data: New York State Department of Health county-level data on tick-borne disease incidence and tick pathogen positivity across eight counties.

Methods: Visualizations in R, with attention to small-denominator reporting problems.

Other work: I contributed literature reviews and manuscript drafting to a randomized controlled trial of tick-control interventions on farms, and made an Alpha-Gal Syndrome resource brochure for farmers.

Output: Poster at Epidemiology Master’s Student Day, Columbia Mailman (Nov 2026).

Population Health Data & Survey Methods

Small-Area Population Estimation for NYC Neighborhoods

Data Analyst Intern · NYC Department of Health, Bureau of Epidemiology Services · Jun – Aug 2026

Question: Which raking approach gives the most reliable demographic estimates for New York City’s Neighborhood Tabulation Areas?

Methods: Raking in SAS, plus processing and validating complex survey data in SAS/SUDAAN (convergence checks and missing-data assessment).

Output: I presented the methodology comparison and my recommended next steps to the Survey Data and Analysis Unit.
